column1: # Player-facing settings: the iOS launcher (dm/ios/Sources/Launcher.swift) and the Mac app's settings window (dm/mac/Launcher.swift) show them before the game starts; Mac front ends read the same list.

# dm/games/settings.py writes one game's list into its app (dm/launcher.json; build_ipa.sh, and dm/mac/pack_app.py through the NSP script): the rows whose condition holds for that game, with its defaults. Each sets an environment variable the host reads when the game starts; one an env file sets
# (Documents/env.txt, the bundle's dm/env.txt) is shown but kept. Diagnostic switches stay environment-only, so they are not listed here. The player's page is docs/settings.md.
#   variable  the environment variable the setting sets

#   kind      choice: values value=label,..., an option only some games have with ?<shown>&<shown> after its label (languages: the game's own, from its control data; every language when it has none, with a note;
#             patches: the values and labels of the profile's setting patches for the variable, setting_patches.tsv); range: values low:high:step, shown as a percentage;
#             toggle: values - (on sets 1, off 0) or <on>/<off>, the two values the variable takes (on/off)
#   default   a value (a toggle's: 1 on, 0 off); DM_GAME_<NAME>: the host's own default from the game profile (game_profile.h, game.py); build:<VAR>: the IPA build's setting (build_ipa.sh)
#             <ios>|<mac> selects the platform's default before resolving a profile macro or build variable
#   shown     always; DM_GAME_<NAME>!=<value> or ==<value>; fixups:<KEY>: main's rewriter table has that key (a stub in the game's build, patch_nso.py);

#             patches:<VAR>: the profile's setting patches (setting_patches.tsv) write words for that variable on the packed build; languages>1 (more than one to pick, so also when the control data lists none); gfxapi:<API>: the packer's GFXAPI;
#             platform:<ios | mac>: the app's platform (SETTINGS_PLATFORM, ios when unset), for a switch only that platform's front end reads; several joined by & must all hold
#   section   Game, Resolution, Effects, Frame rate, HDR, Controls or Performance: a heading on the settings screen. Sections come in the order of their first rows, and rows in table order
#             within each section; <ios>|<mac> gives each platform its own (a row the iPhone keeps under Game, beside Console mode, goes under Resolution in the Mac window)
#             Reset to tested defaults clears all launcher choices; values fixed by an env file stay
#   label, note  the setting's name and the line under it (may be empty; only for a setting with a cost: latency, memory, heat)
#   meta      optional, key=value pairs separated by ; (settings.py META lists the keys; docs/frontends.md, The settings list, describes them):
#             level=basic  a setting a front end shows first;  needs=<VAR>=<value>[|<value>...]  a sub-setting, drawn only while the row that sets <VAR> is drawn and has one of the values
#             conflicts=<VAR>=<value>  held at its default, and drawn disabled, while the row that sets <VAR> has that value; choosing that value resets this row;
#             conflicts=<VAR>=<value>:<own value>[|<own value>...]  only those values of this row: not offered while <VAR> has the value, and reset when it is chosen;
#             atleast=<VAR>  a choice of numbers: only values at least the number the row that sets <VAR> holds are offered; a lower one is raised to the lowest offered
#             rates=<value>:<rate>[|<value>:<rate>...]  a row of upscale rates: its values that are not numbers and the rate each renders at (its render size); at rate 1 such a
#             value keeps the upscaler running, anti-aliasing the output's size
# The Mac window's Resolution section follows the picture's way: what the game upscales to (Output resolution), with what (Game's upscaler; a MetalFX temporal option such as
# camera jitter goes right after it), how much smaller it renders (Render resolution, then Dynamic resolution and its Softest), and the app's own scaling to the window (Upscaling)

column8: Adjusts resolution between 70% and 100% under load. Turn off to keep full resolution for the selected console mode.

Docked, the game upscales once, straight to its window (Game default and Window alike). Experimental: Match display sizes that window to the pixels the picture takes on your screen, chosen at launch: restart after moving the game to another screen or switching between window and fullscreen. Sharper, for more GPU time.
Experimental: moves the camera by under a pixel each frame so the temporal scaler can smooth edges and recover fine detail. Some effects may shimmer.

How much smaller than the output the game renders; with dynamic resolution, the sharpest it renders. Native renders the output itself with the game's own edge smoothing, without its upscaler or MetalFX. Native (MetalFX AA) renders the output itself and MetalFX's temporal scaler smooths it: needs MetalFX temporal, for more GPU time. Ultra performance needs a MetalFX upscaler.
Renders softer when frames run late, down to Softest, and comes back to Render resolution: never sharper.
The furthest dynamic resolution goes when frames run late.

Game samples textures half a level sharper while the game upscales, as on the Switch. NVIDIA (temporal), for MetalFX temporal, follows NVIDIA's guidance for its upscaler: textures sharper by the render resolution, set again at each change, and a level more with Anti-aliasing (jitter). Fine patterns may shimmer, more so without jitter.

column3: 0=0 (the game's at native),-0.5=-0.5 (the game's while upscaling)
column8: With Native (MetalFX AA) and the Game mip bias: -0.5 samples textures half a level sharper, as the game does while it upscales: more texture detail, and more shimmer for the anti-aliasing to settle.
Uses more GPU time and can increase heat.
Full draws ambient occlusion, refraction and soft particles at the render size instead of half: sharper, for more GPU time and memory. Untested.
Full keeps shadows sharp when the game lowers its resolution, for a little more GPU time.
Sharper shadows for more GPU time and memory (the app gives the game's render targets more at launch). Larger sizes are untested: if the game crashes, set it back.
Uses a little more GPU time.

Prefer 60 drops to 30 only while frames are too slow for 60 and tries 60 again every few seconds, so the game keeps its real speed; a scene that cannot hold 60 stutters briefly at each try. Hold 30 stays at 30.
Shows a picture MetalFX makes between two game frames: smoother motion on a 120 Hz screen, about half a frame more latency and more GPU time.
The game's own HDR picture, on a screen with HDR (an XDR screen, or a monitor with High Dynamic Range on in System Settings › Displays).
The brightness of white in the HUD and menus: raise it if the game looks dim next to other windows.

column3: 0=From the screen,400=400 nits,600=600 nits,800=800 nits,1000=1000 nits
column8: Lower it if bright highlights look flat or clipped.
Try Linear if the picture looks washed out or grey.
Try BT.709 if colours look oversaturated.
Fill crops the game's 16:9 picture to cover the screen. Health bars, subtitles or maps near the edges can be cut off. A full-screen picture without cropping needs a patch for each game.
Renders about a quarter more pixels: a little slower and warmer.
Up to one frame more display latency.
Keeps a pipeline archive; uses more memory.
The first start waits a few minutes for it, once.
